Can explain the significance of the Delhi Sultanate for Indian history — it established Muslim rule in north India for over three centuries, introduced new architectural styles (Indo-Islamic), new administrative systems (iqta, zabt), and new cultural elements (Persian language, Sufi traditions), and it connected India to the wider Islamic world of trade and diplomacy — and can explain why this period was a bridge between ancient and Mughal India.

title: Comparative Study of the Khaljis and the Tughlaqs — Policies, Administration and Outcomes
subject: histciv
definition: The comparative study of the Khalji and Tughlaq dynasties examines how two successive ruling houses of the Delhi Sultanate, governing within a single political tradition yet choosing sharply different administrative models, produced opposite outcomes in stability and longevity. The Khalji dynasty, founded by Jalal-ud-din Khalji in 1290 CE and reaching its zenith under Alauddin Khalji (1296-1316), lasted only thirty years yet remained internally coherent throughout Alauddin's twenty-year reign. The Tughlaq dynasty, founded by Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq in 1320 CE and stretching nominally to 1414 CE, governed a larger territory but began fragmenting within the lifetime of its most ambitious ruler, Muhammad bin Tughlaq (1325-1351). The comparison unfolds across at least five dimensions: origin and dynastic duration, territorial expansion, revenue policy, military organisation, and treatment of the nobility. On origin, the Khaljis were of Turkish-Khalaj background and rose by overthrowing the last Mamluk ruler, whereas the Tughlaqs were of Turkish or mixed Turko-Indian origin and seized power after the brief usurpation of Khusrau Khan in 1320. On expansion, Alauddin pushed the Sultanate south of the Vindhyas for the first time through Malik Kafur's tribute campaigns against Devagiri, Warangal and the Hoysalas between 1308 and 1311, while Muhammad bin Tughlaq inherited those conquests and briefly added Daulatabad as a second capital. On revenue, Alauddin imposed direct land measurement known as zabt, claiming half the produce for the state, whereas Muhammad bin Tughlaq raised the Doab tax further during a famine year around 1326, and his successor Firuz Shah Tughlaq (1351-1388) reverted to a gentler iqta-based collection. On military organisation, Alauddin maintained a large standing cavalry cheaply supplied through regulated grain, cloth and horse prices fixed at Delhi's Siri, Mandi and Sarai-i-Adl markets, while Muhammad bin Tughlaq attempted centralised control through administrative experiments rather than price regulation. On treatment of nobles, Alauddin crushed the Chihalgani oligarchy inherited from the Mamluks, banned private noble meetings and confiscated their wealth, whereas Muhammad bin Tughlaq executed or replaced nobles on a mass scale, creating a revolving-door court that undermined loyalty. The decisive contrast lies in outcome: Alauddin's working authoritarianism held the empire together and passed it intact to his successors, while Muhammad's visionary but poorly executed reforms — the 1327 capital shift to Daulatabad, the 1329 token copper currency counterfeited by the mint-master Hausala, and the punitive Doab tax — triggered peasant flight, treasury drain and the secession of Madurai in 1334, Bengal in 1338 and the Bahmani Kingdom in 1347, fragmenting the Sultanate within his own lifetime.
eli5: Imagine two older cousins each given charge of the same big family shop. The first cousin, Alauddin, is strict and bossy but keeps the shop running smoothly for twenty years — he checks the stock himself, fixes the prices so the workers can afford lunch, and fires anyone who cheats. When he steps down, the shop is still in good shape. The second cousin, Muhammad, is clever and full of big ideas — he wants to move the shop to a bigger city, print his own play-money coupons, and charge the farmers extra during a drought. But his ideas are too hard to carry out, the coupons get faked, the farmers run away, and three branch shops break off and open their own stores while he is still in charge. The lesson: a strict plan that actually works beats a brilliant plan that falls apart.

diagnosticQuestions.question: State the approximate date ranges of the Khalji and Tughlaq dynasties, name the founder of each, and identify the main ruler under whom each dynasty reached its peak. Then state one key revenue policy of each peak ruler.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The Khalji dynasty ruled from approximately 1290 to 1320 CE and was founded by Jalal-ud-din Khalji in 1290 CE; its peak ruler was Alauddin Khalji (1296-1316). The Tughlaq dynasty ruled from approximately 1320 to 1414 CE and was founded by Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq in 1320 CE; its peak and most ambitious ruler was Muhammad bin Tughlaq (1325-1351). Alauddin Khalji's key revenue policy was the zabt system of direct land measurement, under which the state claimed fifty per cent of the produce. Muhammad bin Tughlaq's key revenue policy was the enhancement of the tax in the fertile Doab region between the Ganga and the Yamuna around 1326 CE, levied at a time of famine, which drove peasants to abandon their villages and reduced the Doab to barren land. The two revenue systems differed fundamentally: Alauddin's was measurement-based and administratively workable, while Muhammad's was punitive and destabilising.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Why is Alauddin Khalji's market price-control system and Muhammad bin Tughlaq's token currency described as fundamentally different types of economic reform, even though both involved state intervention in the economy? Explain the mechanism and the outcome of each.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Alauddin's market reform and Muhammad bin Tughlaq's token currency were both state interventions, but they differed in mechanism and outcome. Alauddin's market reform fixed the prices of grain, cloth and horses at Delhi's three regulated markets — Siri, Mandi and Sarai-i-Adl — so that his large standing cavalry could be cheaply supplied. The mechanism was administrative enforcement: hoarders were punished, grain prices were fixed at around seven and a half jitals per man, and the system actually functioned for roughly two decades. The outcome was a stable, well-supplied army that could defend Delhi against the Mongol invasions of 1299, 1303 and 1305. Muhammad bin Tughlaq's token currency of 1329 CE substituted copper and brass coins stamped at par with silver tankas, intending to increase the money supply and reduce the drain of silver from the treasury. The mechanism was monetary substitution, but the execution failed because the copper tokens were easy to counterfeit — the Hindu mint-master Hausala and others flooded the market with fakes — and the Sultan was forced to withdraw the tokens and repay silver from the treasury, bankrupting it. The outcome was economic disruption and loss of public trust. Alauddin's reform worked because it relied on enforceable price controls; Muhammad's failed because it relied on a token currency that the state could not protect against counterfeiting.

diagnosticQuestions.question: "The Khalji empire was smaller but more stable, while the Tughlaq empire was larger but collapsed faster." Evaluate this statement with reference to territorial expansion, revenue policy, military organisation, treatment of nobles, and the outcomes under Alauddin Khalji and Muhammad bin Tughlaq. Draw a reasoned conclusion about which administrative model was more effective and why.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The statement is strongly supported by the historical evidence across all five dimensions. On territorial expansion, Alauddin Khalji pushed the Sultanate south of the Vindhyas for the first time through Malik Kafur's tribute campaigns of 1308-1311 against Devagiri, Warangal and the Hoysalas, but the southern territories were tribute-paying rather than fully annexed, keeping the core empire compact and governable. Muhammad bin Tughlaq inherited those conquests and briefly added Daulatabad as a second capital after the 1327 shift, governing a larger territory — but the very size of this empire became a burden when his administrative experiments failed. On revenue policy, Alauddin's zabt system of direct land measurement with a fifty per cent state share was harsh but workable, generating reliable income without provoking mass peasant flight. Muhammad bin Tughlaq's enhanced Doab tax of around 1326, levied during a famine, drove peasants to abandon their villages and reduced a fertile region to barren land, destroying the revenue base he sought to strengthen. On military organisation, Alauddin maintained a large standing cavalry cheaply supplied through his regulated market system, producing an army that successfully repelled the Mongol invasions of 1299, 1303 and 1305. Muhammad bin Tughlaq attempted centralised military control through administrative restructuring rather than price regulation, but the absence of a working supply system left his army overstretched across a larger empire. On treatment of nobles, Alauddin crushed the surviving noble oligarchy by banning private meetings and confiscating wealth, creating a subdued but loyal court. Muhammad bin Tughlaq executed and replaced nobles on a mass scale, producing a revolving-door court in which loyalty evaporated and provincial governors saw no reason to remain obedient. On outcome, the contrast is decisive: Alauddin's empire lasted twenty years under his personal rule and was handed to his successors intact, while Muhammad bin Tughlaq's empire fragmented within his own lifetime with the secession of Madurai in 1334, Bengal in 1338 and the Bahmani Kingdom in 1347. The reasoned conclusion is that Alauddin's authoritarian-but-workable model was more effective than Muhammad's visionary-but-broken model, because the effectiveness of an administrative system depends not on the brilliance of its ideas but on the state's capacity to implement them. A harsh system that functions is superior to a brilliant system that collapses, and the Khalji-Tughlaq comparison demonstrates that ambition without implementation capacity produces fragmentation rather than progress.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Imagine you are a Class 7 student preparing a comparison chart for the ICSE board examination. Construct a two-column table with five rows — Origin, Revenue, Economic Reform, Treatment of Nobles, Outcome — filling the Khalji column with Alauddin's policies and the Tughlaq column with Muhammad bin Tughlaq's policies. Then write a one-sentence evaluative verdict at the bottom of the chart.
diagnosticQuestions.answer:
Two-column comparison chart — Khalji vs Tughlaq:
| Dimension | Khalji (Alauddin Khalji, 1296-1316) | Tughlaq (Muhammad bin Tughlaq, 1325-1351) |
| Origin | Turkish-Khalaj; overthrew the last Mamluk in 1290 | Turkish or Turko-Indian; seized power after Khusrau Khan in 1320 |
| Revenue | Zabt direct land measurement; 50 per cent state share | Enhanced Doab tax during famine around 1326; peasant flight |
| Economic Reform | Market price controls for grain, cloth, horses at Delhi | Token copper currency of 1329; counterfeited by Hausala |
| Treatment of Nobles | Crushed noble oligarchy; banned private meetings; confiscated wealth | Mass executions and replacements of nobles; loyalty evaporated |
| Outcome | Stable 20-year reign; empire passed intact to successors | Fragmented within his lifetime; Madurai 1334, Bengal 1338, Bahmani 1347 seceded |
One-sentence evaluative verdict: The Khalji model was harsh but workable, producing a stable empire that outlived its founder, while the Tughlaq model was visionary but broken, producing a larger empire that fragmented during its main ruler's own reign.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a short historical argument (150-200 words) in which you take the position that Muhammad bin Tughlaq's experiments were not "mad" but were visionary reforms that failed due to poor implementation capacity. Reference at least three of his experiments, explain the reasoning behind each, and contrast the reasoning with the outcome. Then state one lesson a modern Indian policymaker could draw from this comparison.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Muhammad bin Tughlaq's experiments were not the work of a madman but of a visionary ruler whose ideas outran his state's capacity to implement them. His transfer of the capital from Delhi to Daulatabad in 1327 was strategically reasoned: a southern capital would better govern the Deccan territories inherited from Alauddin Khalji and provide a second base against Mongol threats from the north-west. The outcome, however, was immense suffering during the 700-mile march and a reversal within eight years. His token copper currency of 1329 was economically reasoned: substituting cheap copper for silver would increase the money supply and conserve the treasury's silver. The outcome was counterfeiting by Hausala and other minters, because the state lacked the technology to make the tokens unforgeable, forcing a humiliating withdrawal. His enhanced Doab tax of 1326 was fiscally reasoned: the fertile Doab could yield more revenue to fund his large empire. The outcome was peasant flight during a famine, because the tax was collected ruthlessly without regard for the harvest failure. The lesson for a modern Indian policymaker is clear: the soundness of a policy's reasoning matters less than the state's capacity to implement it without harming the people it governs, and ambition without implementation capacity produces suffering rather than progress.

Can evaluate why the Khalji empire under Alauddin remained stable and was passed intact to his successors (because his authoritarian system was well-enforced and his military was well-supplied), while the Tughlaq empire under Muhammad bin Tughlaq fragmented within his own lifetime with the secession of Madurai (1334 CE), Bengal (1338 CE), and the Bahmani Kingdom (1347 CE) — and can explain why fragmentation occurred (Muhammad's failed experiments eroded the loyalty of provincial governors, who saw independence as safer than continued service).

5. Can draw a reasoned conclusion about which administrative model was more effective — Alauddin's working authoritarianism (which produced stability at the cost of peasant suffering) was more effective at maintaining the empire, while Muhammad's visionary but poorly executed reforms (which aimed at grand goals but failed in implementation) were more ambitious but less practical — and can explain why execution matters more than vision in governance.
