title: Supreme Court — Jurisdiction, Judicial Review, Court of Record and Writs
subject: histciv
definition: The Supreme Court of India is the highest judicial authority in the Republic and exercises five distinct types of jurisdiction that together enable it to administer justice, enforce fundamental rights, and uphold the Constitution. Original jurisdiction, defined under Article 131, allows the Supreme Court to directly hear disputes between the Government of India and one or more states, or between two or more states — for example, the Cauvery water dispute between Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, adjudicated directly because no lower court can settle conflicts between constituent units of the Union. Appellate jurisdiction, governed by Articles 132 to 134 and Article 136, empowers the Court to hear appeals from High Courts in constitutional matters (Article 132), civil matters (Article 133), and criminal matters (Article 134); Article 136 grants Special Leave to Appeal, a discretionary power to grant permission to appeal from any court or tribunal in India. The Shah Bano case of 1985, in which a divorced Muslim woman's right to maintenance was upheld on appeal, is a landmark example. Advisory or Revisory jurisdiction, established under Article 143, permits the President to refer any question of law or fact of public importance to the Supreme Court for its opinion; the Court examined the Ram Janmabhoomi dispute through this route in 2019, and earlier references included the Berubari Union case of 1960. The advisory opinion is not binding on the government — it is constitutional counsel, not a judicial command. Judicial Review, rooted in Article 13, is the power to examine the constitutionality of any law passed by Parliament or a state legislature, and any executive action, and to strike down anything that violates the Constitution. In the Kesavananda Bharati case of 1973, the Court established the basic structure doctrine, holding that Parliament may amend the Constitution but cannot alter its basic structure; in the Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain case of 1975, the Court struck down the 39th Constitutional Amendment that tried to place the Prime Minister's election beyond judicial scrutiny; and in the Puttaswamy judgment of 2017, the Court affirmed the right to privacy as a fundamental right under Article 21. As a Court of Record, declared under Article 129, the Supreme Court's decisions are permanent legal records and binding precedents for all lower courts under the doctrine of stare decisis. Through writs issued under Article 32, the Court directly enforces fundamental rights; Dr B.R. Ambedkar called Article 32 the "heart and soul" of the Constitution because it provides the remedy through which every other fundamental right can be enforced. The five writs are Habeas Corpus ("produce the body" — directing the state to produce a detained person and justify the detention), Mandamus ("we command" — directing a public official to perform a legal duty), Prohibition (stopping a lower court from proceeding beyond its jurisdiction), Certiorari ("to certify" — quashing an order of a lower court or tribunal), and Quo Warranto ("by what authority" — questioning a person's authority to hold a public office). During the Emergency of 1976, the ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla case saw the Court controversially refuse to issue Habeas Corpus to detained citizens — a decision widely regarded as the darkest chapter in Indian judicial history and one finally overruled in the Puttaswamy case of 2017.
eli5: Imagine the Supreme Court is the principal's office of the entire country's school system. Original jurisdiction means the principal directly settles fights between two prefects (states). Appellate jurisdiction means a student can appeal to the principal if a teacher's punishment seems unfair. Advisory jurisdiction means the school's managing committee can ask the principal for advice on a tricky rule — but the principal's advice is just advice, not a command. Judicial review means the principal can cancel any prefect's rule that breaks the school handbook. Writs are special stamped letters the principal sends to fix specific wrongs — like ordering a teacher to produce a student they locked up (Habeas Corpus) or commanding a clerk to issue a delayed passport (Mandamus).

diagnosticQuestions.question: Define the five types of jurisdiction exercised by the Supreme Court of India, citing the relevant constitutional article for each. Then define a writ and list the five writs with their Latin meanings.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The Supreme Court exercises five types of jurisdiction. Original jurisdiction under Article 131 allows the Court to directly hear disputes between the Centre and one or more states, or between states — e.g. the Cauvery water dispute. Appellate jurisdiction under Articles 132-134 allows appeals from High Courts in constitutional (Article 132), civil (Article 133), and criminal (Article 134) matters; Article 136 grants Special Leave to Appeal, a discretionary power to appeal from any court or tribunal. Advisory jurisdiction under Article 143 allows the President to refer questions of law or fact of public importance for the Court's opinion; this opinion is not binding. Judicial Review under Article 13 empowers the Court to examine the constitutionality of any law or executive action and strike down violations. Court of Record under Article 129 means the Court's decisions are permanent legal records and binding precedents for all lower courts. A writ is a formal written order issued by a court directing a person, official, or government body to do or refrain from a specific act. The five writs are: Habeas Corpus ("produce the body" — unlawful detention), Mandamus ("we command" — official inaction), Prohibition (stopping a lower court from exceeding jurisdiction), Certiorari ("to certify" — quashing a lower court's order), and Quo Warranto ("by what authority" — questioning authority to hold public office).

diagnosticQuestions.question: Why did Dr B.R. Ambedkar describe Article 32 as the "heart and soul" of the Constitution? Explain how the five writs under Article 32 give operational force to the fundamental rights guaranteed in Part III, and explain why the advisory opinion under Article 143 is not binding on the government even though it comes from the highest court in the land.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Dr B.R. Ambedkar called Article 32 the "heart and soul" of the Constitution because it provides the constitutional remedy through which every other fundamental right is enforced. Without Article 32, the fundamental rights in Part III — equality, freedom of speech, life and personal liberty — would remain mere declarations with no mechanism for enforcement. Article 32 empowers a citizen to move the Supreme Court directly, and the Court can issue any of the five writs. Each writ addresses a specific violation: Habeas Corpus protects personal liberty by requiring the state to justify detention; Mandamus compels a public official to perform a legal duty, so that a citizen whose rights depend on official action is not left helpless by inaction; Prohibition and Certiorari ensure lower courts do not exceed jurisdiction or issue unlawful orders; Quo Warranto ensures public offices are not held without legal authority. Together, these writs transform fundamental rights from abstract guarantees into enforceable protections. The advisory opinion under Article 143 is not binding because advisory jurisdiction differs fundamentally from judicial jurisdiction. In a judicial case, two parties present opposing arguments, the Court resolves a live dispute, and its judgment is binding. In an advisory reference, there is no dispute between parties — the President asks for the Court's legal opinion on a question of public importance. Because there is no lis (dispute) and no parties to be bound, the opinion carries great persuasive weight but is not a legally binding command. This preserves the separation of powers: the judiciary advises, but the executive and legislature retain their discretion to act on or decline that advice.

diagnosticQuestions.question: "Judicial review is the most powerful check the Supreme Court exercises over Parliament and the executive, but it is also self-limited by the doctrines of judicial restraint and the basic structure." Evaluate this statement with reference to the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973), the Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain case (1975), and the Puttaswamy case (2017). Argue whether judicial review strengthens or weakens Indian democracy, and explain how the basic structure doctrine both empowers and limits the Court.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The statement accurately captures the dual character of judicial review — simultaneously the Supreme Court's most powerful check on the political branches and a power constrained by the Court's own doctrines. Judicial review under Article 13 empowers the Court to strike down any law or executive action that violates the Constitution. In the Kesavananda Bharati case of 1973, the Court ruled that Parliament's power to amend the Constitution under Article 368 is not unlimited — Parliament may amend but cannot alter the "basic structure," which includes the rule of law, separation of powers, judicial review, fundamental rights, and the democratic and secular character of the Republic. This doctrine was tested in the Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain case of 1975, where the Court struck down the 39th Amendment that had placed the Prime Minister's election beyond judicial scrutiny, holding that it violated the basic structure by destroying the rule of law and free and fair elections. In the Puttaswamy case of 2017, the Court affirmed the right to privacy as a fundamental right under Article 21, overruling the ADM Jabalpur decision of 1976. Judicial review strengthens Indian democracy because it ensures that no law or executive action can override the Constitution's guarantees of equality, liberty, and due process. Without it, a parliamentary majority could pass laws stripping minorities of their rights. However, judicial review is self-limited. The doctrine of judicial restraint holds that the Court should not interfere in policy matters within the domain of the legislature and executive, and should intervene only when a clear constitutional violation is shown. The basic structure doctrine both empowers and limits the Court: it empowers the Court to strike down even constitutional amendments that destroy the Constitution's core, but it also limits the Court by requiring it to ground decisions in identifiable constitutional principles rather than personal preference. This balance — powerful but principled — makes judicial review a stabilising force in Indian democracy.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A citizen named Ramesh has been detained by the police for three weeks without being told the reason and without being produced before a magistrate. Using your knowledge of writs under Article 32, identify which writ Ramesh's family should file in the Supreme Court, explain what the writ means and what it would require the state to do, and explain why this writ was controversially refused during the Emergency of 1976 in the ADM Jabalpur case.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Ramesh's family should file a Habeas Corpus petition under Article 32 in the Supreme Court. Habeas Corpus means "produce the body" — a writ directing the state to produce Ramesh before the Court and justify the detention by showing a lawful cause. If the state cannot demonstrate a legal basis, the Court will order his release. Habeas Corpus is the most direct protection of personal liberty because it places the burden on the state to justify any deprivation of freedom. During the Emergency of 1976, in A.D.M. Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla, the Supreme Court controversially held that when the right to move courts for enforcement of fundamental rights under Article 21 is suspended during an Emergency, even Habeas Corpus cannot be issued. This meant thousands of political detainees had no judicial remedy. The decision was passed by four judges to one, with Justice H.R. Khanna dissenting that the right to life and personal liberty cannot be entirely suspended even during an Emergency. This dissent cost him the position of Chief Justice of India, but it was vindicated when the Puttaswamy case of 2017 explicitly overruled the ADM Jabalpur decision. In Ramesh's case, since India is not under a declared Emergency today, his family's Habeas Corpus petition would be maintainable, and the Court would require the police to produce Ramesh and justify the detention.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a one-page revision chart for the Supreme Court's jurisdiction and writs. For each of the five types of jurisdiction, provide the constitutional article, a one-line definition, and one Indian example. For each of the five writs, provide the Latin meaning and a one-line example of when it would be used. Then write a 100-word closing paragraph explaining why Article 32 was called the "heart and soul" of the Constitution by Dr B.R. Ambedkar.
diagnosticQuestions.answer:
Revision chart for the Supreme Court of India:

JURISDICTION:
1. Original Jurisdiction — Article 131 — The Court directly hears disputes between the Centre and states or between states. Example: Cauvery water dispute between Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.
2. Appellate Jurisdiction — Articles 132-134, 136 — The Court hears appeals from High Courts in constitutional, civil, and criminal matters; Special Leave to Appeal under Article 136. Example: Shah Bano case (1985).
3. Advisory/Revisory Jurisdiction — Article 143 — The President refers questions of law or fact of public importance to the Court; opinion is not binding. Example: Ram Janmabhoomi reference (2019).
4. Judicial Review — Article 13 — The Court examines the constitutionality of laws and executive actions and strikes down violations. Example: Kesavananda Bharati case (1973), basic structure doctrine.
5. Court of Record — Article 129 — The Court's decisions are permanent legal records and binding precedents for all lower courts. Example: Kesavananda Bharati ruling continues to bind all courts.

WRITS:
1. Habeas Corpus — "Produce the body" — Issued when a person is unlawfully detained; the Court orders the state to produce the detainee and justify the detention. Example: A man held by police for three weeks without charge.
2. Mandamus — "We command" — Issued when a public official fails to perform a legal duty. Example: A passport officer who unreasonably delays issuing a passport.
3. Prohibition — "To prohibit" — Issued to stop a lower court from proceeding with a case beyond its jurisdiction. Example: A sessions court hearing a matter outside its jurisdiction.
4. Certiorari — "To certify" — Issued to quash an order already made by a lower court or tribunal. Example: A tribunal cancelling a licence without giving the affected party a hearing.
5. Quo Warranto — "By what authority" — Issued to question a person's authority to hold a public office. Example: A person appointed as a district officer without the required qualifications.

Closing paragraph: Dr B.R. Ambedkar called Article 32 the "heart and soul" of the Constitution because it provides the constitutional remedy through which every fundamental right is enforced. Without Article 32, the rights to equality, freedom, and life would be mere declarations with no mechanism for enforcement. The five writs transform these rights from abstract guarantees into practical protections, giving the Supreme Court the power to order the state to produce a detainee, compel an official to act, stop a lower court from exceeding its authority, quash an unlawful order, or question an illegal appointment. This is why Article 32 gives the Constitution its living force.

masteryCriteria: Can define and distinguish the five types of jurisdiction — Original (Centre-state and inter-state disputes under Article 131, e.g. the Cauvery water dispute), Appellate (appeals from High Courts under Articles 132-134 and Special Leave to Appeal under Article 136, e.g. the Shah Bano case of 1985), Revisory/Advisory (President's reference under Article 143, e.g. the Ram Janmabhoomi reference of 2019, opinion non-binding), Judicial Review (power to examine constitutionality under Article 13, e.g. the Kesavananda Bharati case of 1973 and the basic structure doctrine), and Court of Record (binding precedents under Article 129). Can define a writ as a formal written order issued by the Court and can list and explain at least four of the five writs — Habeas Corpus ("produce the body" — unlawful detention), Mandamus ("we command" — official inaction), Prohibition (stopping a lower court from exceeding jurisdiction), Certiorari ("to certify" — quashing a lower court's order), and Quo Warranto ("by what authority" — questioning authority to hold public office). Can explain that Article 32 provides the right to constitutional remedies and that Dr B.R. Ambedkar called it the "heart and soul" of the Constitution.

title: The High Court — Composition, Jurisdiction and Writs
subject: histciv
definition: The High Court is the highest judicial authority in a state or group of states in India, established under Article 214 of the Constitution, which mandates that there shall be a High Court for each state. Article 215 designates every High Court as a Court of Record whose judgments serve as binding precedents for all subordinate courts within its territorial jurisdiction. As of 2025, there are 25 High Courts in India, some serving individual states and others serving groups of states or union territories. The composition of a High Court, laid down by Article 216, consists of a Chief Justice and such other judges as the President may appoint; the sanctioned strength varies by court, with the Allahabad High Court (established 1866) having the largest sanctioned strength of 160 judges, while smaller High Courts may have fewer than twenty. The appointment of High Court judges is governed by Article 217: the Chief Justice of a High Court is appointed by the President in consultation with the Chief Justice of India, the Governor of the state, and the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court, and other judges are appointed by the President on the advice of the collegium system. To qualify as a High Court judge, a person must be a citizen of India and must have held a judicial office in India for at least ten years, or must have been an advocate of a High Court for at least ten years. The retirement age for High Court judges is 62, three years younger than the retirement age of 65 for Supreme Court judges. The High Court exercises five types of jurisdiction. Original jurisdiction allows certain cases to be filed directly in the High Court, such as company law matters, writ petitions, and cases involving constitutional interpretation; the Bombay High Court (established 1862) exercises original jurisdiction over Mumbai. Appellate jurisdiction enables the High Court to hear appeals from subordinate courts, including district and sessions courts, in both civil and criminal matters. Revisory jurisdiction, supported by Article 227's power of superintendence, allows the High Court to call for the records of any subordinate court to examine the correctness, legality, or propriety of its proceedings. Judicial Review empowers the High Court to examine the constitutionality of state laws and executive actions, striking down those that violate the Constitution. As a Court of Record, its decisions bind all subordinate courts. Most significantly, under Article 226, every High Court has the power to issue all five constitutional writs — Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, and Quo Warranto — not only for the enforcement of fundamental rights, as the Supreme Court does under Article 32, but also for the enforcement of any other legal right, making Article 226 broader in scope than Article 32. Justice Anna Chandy, appointed to the Kerala High Court in 1959, was the first woman to serve as a High Court judge in India. In the Himmat Lal Sharma v. Commissioner of Police, Ahmedabad case (1972), the Gujarat High Court used its Article 226 writ jurisdiction to strike down a police notification restricting public meetings, demonstrating that High Courts protect not only fundamental rights but also ordinary legal rights of citizens.
eli5: Imagine your school has a Principal at the top (the Supreme Court at New Delhi) and each branch campus (each state) has a Head Teacher (the High Court). The Head Teacher can solve problems for students at that branch — unfair marks, denied scholarships, broken rules — and can also check that class teachers are doing their jobs right. The Principal (Supreme Court) can only step in for very big rights issues (under Article 32, for Fundamental Rights violations), but the Head Teacher (High Court under Article 226) can help with both big and small rights problems, including not just Fundamental Rights but also any other legal right. That is why the Head Teacher, like the High Court, is the court most people actually approach for help. High Courts have a Chief Justice and other judges (the number varies by state — Allahabad has the most with over 100), appointed by the President in consultation with the Chief Justice of India and the Governor. They can issue five types of writs: habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, and quo warranto.

diagnosticQuestions.question: State the qualifications required to become a High Court judge, the retirement age, and the number of High Courts in India as of 2025. Name the articles of the Constitution that govern the composition and appointment of High Court judges.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: To be appointed as a High Court judge under Article 217, a person must be a citizen of India and must satisfy one of two conditions: either the person must have held a judicial office in India for at least ten years, or the person must have been an advocate of a High Court for at least ten years. The retirement age for High Court judges is 62, three years younger than the retirement age of 65 for Supreme Court judges. As of 2025, there are 25 High Courts in India, some serving individual states and others serving groups of states or union territories. Article 214 mandates that there shall be a High Court for each state. Article 216 states that every High Court consists of a Chief Justice and such other judges as the President may appoint. Article 217 governs the appointment, qualifications, and retirement of High Court judges. The Chief Justice of a High Court is appointed by the President in consultation with the Chief Justice of India, the Governor of the state, and the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court, while other judges are appointed by the President on the collegium's advice. The sanctioned strength varies by court, with the Allahabad High Court (established 1866) having the largest sanctioned strength of 160 judges.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Explain why Article 226 is considered broader in scope than Article 32, and why this difference matters for ordinary citizens. Refer to the Himmat Lal Sharma case (1972) in your answer.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Article 32 empowers the Supreme Court to issue all five writs — Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, and Quo Warranto — but only for the enforcement of fundamental rights guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution, such as the right to equality, the right to freedom, and the right to life and personal liberty. Article 226 empowers every High Court to issue the same five writs for two purposes: first, for the enforcement of fundamental rights, and second, for the enforcement of any other legal right — any right conferred by ordinary law passed by Parliament or a state legislature. This makes Article 226 broader than Article 32 because its scope extends beyond fundamental rights to cover all legal rights. The practical significance is enormous: an ordinary citizen whose fundamental rights have not been violated but who has been denied a legal right — such as a pension owed under a government scheme, a minimum wage guaranteed by labour law, or a licence wrongly refused under a statutory regulation — can approach the High Court under Article 226 but cannot approach the Supreme Court directly under Article 32. The Himmat Lal Sharma v. Commissioner of Police, Ahmedabad case (1972) illustrates this: the Gujarat High Court used its Article 226 writ jurisdiction to strike down a police notification restricting public meetings, protecting a legal right that was not necessarily a fundamental right in the strict Article 32 sense. This demonstrates that High Courts serve as the most accessible constitutional remedy for citizens facing administrative injustice, because they can correct violations of both fundamental and legal rights, while the Supreme Court's Article 32 jurisdiction is confined to fundamental rights alone.

diagnosticQuestions.question: "The High Court is more accessible to the ordinary citizen than the Supreme Court, and its writ jurisdiction under Article 226 is therefore more important for the protection of citizens' rights than Article 32." Evaluate this statement with reference to the composition, jurisdiction, and writ powers of the High Court, the scope of Article 226 compared to Article 32, and the role of the High Court as a Court of Record. Argue whether the High Court's writ jurisdiction is indeed more important for citizens or whether both articles are equally important.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The statement is largely supported by the constitutional design and practical realities of access to justice, though both Article 226 and Article 32 serve essential and complementary roles. The High Court is the highest judicial authority in a state, established under Article 214, and there are 25 High Courts across India as of 2025, meaning that a High Court is geographically accessible to citizens in every part of the country. The Supreme Court, by contrast, sits only in New Delhi, making direct access costly and impractical for most citizens. This geographical reality alone makes the High Court the court that most citizens approach for constitutional remedies. The writ jurisdiction of the High Court under Article 226 is broader in scope than the Supreme Court's Article 32 because Article 226 covers not only fundamental rights but also any other legal right, while Article 32 is confined to fundamental rights alone. A citizen denied a pension, a government job, or a statutory licence — where no fundamental right is directly involved — can approach the High Court but not the Supreme Court under its writ jurisdiction. The Himmat Lal Sharma v. Commissioner of Police, Ahmedabad case (1972) demonstrates this: the Gujarat High Court struck down a police notification restricting public meetings under Article 226, protecting a legal right that fell outside the strict scope of Article 32. The High Court also exercises Original, Appellate, Revisory, and Judicial Review jurisdiction, and serves as a Court of Record under Article 215 whose decisions bind all subordinate courts in the state. This combination of broad jurisdiction and geographical accessibility makes the High Court the primary guardian of citizens' rights at the state level. However, it would be inaccurate to say that Article 32 is less important. Article 32, described by Dr B R Ambedkar as the "heart and soul of the Constitution," provides a direct constitutional remedy for fundamental rights violations and allows citizens to approach the Supreme Court directly. The Supreme Court also serves as the final court of appeal, ensuring uniformity in the interpretation of fundamental rights across the nation. The two articles are complementary: Article 226 provides broader and more accessible remedies at the state level, while Article 32 provides a direct remedy at the apex level and ensures national consistency. In conclusion, for the ordinary citizen, the High Court's writ jurisdiction under Article 226 is indeed more accessible and broader in scope, making it the more frequently invoked remedy; but both articles are equally important in the constitutional scheme, as they together ensure that no violation of any right — fundamental or legal — goes without a judicial remedy.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student in Karnataka is denied a government scholarship that she is legally entitled to under a state education scheme, but no fundamental right appears to have been violated. Using your knowledge of High Court jurisdiction and Article 226, advise her on which court she should approach, what remedy she should seek, and why she cannot approach the Supreme Court directly under Article 32 for this grievance.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The student should approach the Karnataka High Court, which is the highest judicial authority in the state. She should file a writ petition under Article 226, seeking the writ of Mandamus — a command issued by the court to a public authority to perform its legal duty. The Mandamus would direct the government to release the scholarship she is legally entitled to under the state education scheme. She can approach the High Court under Article 226 because it empowers every High Court to issue writs not only for the enforcement of fundamental rights but also for the enforcement of any other legal right — any right conferred by ordinary law, including the right to a scholarship under a state scheme. Even though no fundamental right under Part III appears to have been violated, her legal right has been infringed, and Article 226 covers such situations. She cannot approach the Supreme Court directly under Article 32 because Article 32 empowers the Supreme Court to issue writs only for the enforcement of fundamental rights, not for other legal rights. Since her case involves a legal right under a state scheme rather than a fundamental right, Article 32 does not provide a direct remedy. The Karnataka High Court has used its writ jurisdiction in similar cases — in 2022, it used its Article 226 powers to direct the government on civic issues — demonstrating that High Courts actively protect citizens' legal rights. She should file her petition with supporting documents showing her eligibility and the government's refusal.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a comparison table that contrasts the High Court and the Supreme Court across six dimensions — constitutional article establishing the court, number of courts, composition and appointment, retirement age of judges, writ jurisdiction article and scope, and types of jurisdiction exercised. Then write a 100-word closing paragraph explaining why the framers of the Constitution gave High Courts broader writ powers than the Supreme Court.
diagnosticQuestions.answer:
Comparison table: High Court vs Supreme Court of India

1. Constitutional article: The Supreme Court is established under Article 124; each High Court is established under Article 214, with Article 215 designating it as a Court of Record.
2. Number of courts: There is one Supreme Court in New Delhi; there are 25 High Courts in India as of 2025, located across the states and union territories.
3. Composition and appointment: The Supreme Court consists of a Chief Justice and 33 other judges, appointed by the President on the collegium's advice; each High Court consists of a Chief Justice and other judges whose number varies (the Allahabad High Court has 160 sanctioned), appointed by the President under Article 217.
4. Retirement age: Supreme Court judges retire at 65; High Court judges retire at 62.
5. Writ jurisdiction: The Supreme Court issues writs under Article 32 for fundamental rights only; High Courts issue writs under Article 226 for both fundamental rights and any other legal right, making Article 226 broader.
6. Types of jurisdiction: Both exercise Original, Appellate, Revisory, Judicial Review, and Court of Record jurisdiction, but the Supreme Court's Original jurisdiction extends to Centre-state disputes (Article 131), while the High Court's Original jurisdiction covers cases filed directly within the state.

Closing paragraph: The framers gave High Courts broader writ powers under Article 226 than the Supreme Court under Article 32 because High Courts are geographically closer to the people and can address a wider range of grievances, including violations of legal rights that do not rise to the level of fundamental rights. With 25 High Courts across the country, citizens in every state have accessible judicial remedies for administrative injustices — denied pensions, refused licences, illegal demolitions — that no fundamental right clause directly addresses. The Supreme Court, sitting only in New Delhi, is reserved as the final guardian of fundamental rights and the ultimate court of appeal. This design balances accessibility with constitutional supremacy.

masteryCriteria: Can state that each state or group of states has a High Court as its highest court, with 25 High Courts in India as of 2025, and that each consists of a Chief Justice and other judges appointed by the President on the collegium's advice under Articles 216 and 217. Can list the qualifications for a High Court judge — citizenship of India plus either ten years as a High Court advocate or ten years holding a judicial office — and state that the retirement age is 62, three years younger than the Supreme Court's 65. Can describe the five types of High Court jurisdiction — Original (cases filed directly, such as writ petitions and company law matters), Appellate (appeals from subordinate courts), Revisory (examining subordinate court records under Article 227), Judicial Review (examining the constitutionality of state laws), and Court of Record (decisions binding all subordinate courts under Article 215). Can explain that High Courts issue all five writs under Article 226, which is broader than the Supreme Court's Article 32 because it covers both fundamental rights and any other legal right, as illustrated by the Himmat Lal Sharma case (1972).

title: Aims and Principles of the United Nations
subject: histciv
definition: The United Nations (UN) is the world's largest intergovernmental organisation, founded on 24 October 1945 when the UN Charter was ratified by the five permanent members of the Security Council — China, France, the USSR, the United Kingdom, and the United States — and a majority of the other signatories. The Charter was drafted at the San Francisco Conference, held from April to June 1945, where 50 nations signed the document; Poland, unable to attend, signed later, bringing the total founding members to 51. India was among the original 50 signatories, represented by Sir Arcot Ramaswamy Mudaliar, and became a founding member when the UN came into existence on 24 October 1945 — a date now observed every year as UN Day. The UN replaced the League of Nations, established in 1919 after World War I but failed to prevent a second global conflict. The League's inability to stop Japan's invasion of Manchuria in 1931 or Italy's invasion of Abyssinia (modern Ethiopia) in 1935 exposed its weakness, and World War II (1939-1945), which killed an estimated 70 to 85 million people, demonstrated the catastrophic cost of that failure. The UN Charter, functioning as the constitution of the organisation, states four aims in Article 1: to maintain international peace and security through collective action; to develop friendly relations among nations based on respect for equal rights and self-determination of peoples; to achieve international cooperation in solving economic, social, cultural, and humanitarian problems; and to be a centre for harmonising the actions of nations in attaining these common ends. Article 2 lays down the principles of conduct: the organisation is based on the sovereign equality of all its members, meaning every nation — large or small — has equal legal standing; all members shall settle their international disputes by peaceful means; all members shall refrain from the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state; and all members shall give the United Nations every assistance in any action it takes. India's commitment to these aims is reflected in Article 51 of the Indian Constitution, a Directive Principle of State Policy, which directs the State to promote international peace and security, maintain just and honourable relations between nations, and foster respect for international law. India has been one of the largest contributors to UN peacekeeping, sending over 200,000 troops to more than 40 missions since 1948. The UN today serves 193 member states as a permanent global forum for peace, development, human rights, and international law.
eli5: Imagine your class has no rules and two big fights broke out last year because nobody could stop them (World War I and World War II). So all the classes in the school send one representative each to a meeting, where they write a charter — a promise sheet. The charter says what they all want (peace, friendship, helping each other) and the rules everyone must follow (treat every class equally, sort out fights by talking not punching, help the school council). That promise sheet, signed on 24 October 1945 by 51 countries including India, is the United Nations Charter. The UN has six main parts: the General Assembly (where all countries meet), the Security Council (the 15-member body that can send peacekeepers), the International Court of Justice (the world court at The Hague), the Secretariat (the staff), the Economic and Social Council, and the Trusteeship Council. The UN replaced the failed League of Nations, which could not stop World War II because it had no army and the USA never joined.

diagnosticQuestions.question: State the full name of the UN, the year and date it was founded, the name and dates of the conference where the Charter was signed, the number of founding members, and the five permanent members of the Security Council. List at least four aims and four principles of the UN as given in the Charter, citing the relevant articles.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The full name is the United Nations, founded on 24 October 1945 when the UN Charter was ratified by the five permanent members and a majority of other signatories. The Charter was signed at the San Francisco Conference, held from April to June 1945, where 50 nations signed; Poland signed later, making 51 founding members. India was among the original 50 signatories. The five permanent members of the Security Council are China, France, the USSR (now Russia), the United Kingdom, and the United States. Article 1 of the Charter states four aims: to maintain international peace and security through collective action; to develop friendly relations among nations based on respect for equal rights and self-determination of peoples; to achieve international cooperation in solving economic, social, cultural, and humanitarian problems; and to be a centre for harmonising the actions of nations in attaining these common ends. Article 2 states the principles: the organisation is based on the sovereign equality of all its members; all members shall settle their international disputes by peaceful means; all members shall refrain from the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state; and all members shall give the United Nations every assistance in any action it takes.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Why did the United Nations replace the League of Nations after World War II? Explain the specific failures of the League that demonstrated its weakness, and explain why the UN Charter's aims and principles were designed to address those failures. Distinguish between aims and principles and explain why both are necessary.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The League of Nations, founded in 1919 after World War I, was the first permanent intergovernmental organisation dedicated to maintaining world peace, but it failed in two critical test cases. First, when Japan invaded Manchuria in 1931, the League condemned the action but Japan simply left the organisation and retained the territory; the League had no military force and no mechanism to compel compliance. Second, when Italy invaded Abyssinia (modern Ethiopia) in 1935, the League imposed limited economic sanctions but excluded key resources like oil, and several members continued trading with Italy; the sanctions failed and Abyssinia was conquered. These failures showed that the League lacked enforcement power, lacked universal membership (the United States never joined), and lacked a binding commitment from members to act collectively. World War II (1939-1945), which killed an estimated 70 to 85 million people, was the ultimate proof of the League's failure. The UN was designed to correct these weaknesses: its aim of maintaining international peace and security (Article 1) directly addresses the League's inability to stop aggression; its principle that all members shall refrain from the threat or use of force (Article 2) creates a binding rule the League lacked; its principle of assistance to the UN means members must support collective action, not ignore it as they did with the League's sanctions; and the Security Council with its five permanent members was designed to ensure that the major powers remain engaged rather than walking away as Japan did in 1931. Aims and principles are both necessary because aims state what the organisation wants to achieve (the destination) while principles state how members must behave to reach those goals (the rules of the road); without aims, the organisation has no purpose, and without principles, the aims cannot be enforced. A charter with only aims would be a wish list; a charter with only principles would be a rulebook with no stated purpose.

diagnosticQuestions.question: "The United Nations Charter's principle of sovereign equality ensures that no single nation can legally dominate others, but the veto power of the five permanent members of the Security Council undermines this principle in practice." Evaluate this statement with reference to the founding of the UN (San Francisco Conference, 1945), the four aims and four principles of the Charter, the failure of the League of Nations, and India's role as a founding member. Argue whether the veto power is a necessary compromise or a fundamental contradiction of the UN's stated principles.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The statement captures a genuine tension at the heart of the United Nations, and the historical evidence supports the view that the veto power is both a necessary compromise and a practical contradiction of sovereign equality — a duality reflecting the political realities of 1945 rather than an avoidable design flaw. The UN was founded on 24 October 1945 after the San Francisco Conference (April-June 1945), where 50 nations signed the Charter (Poland later, making 51 founding members), including India as a founding member. The Charter's Article 1 states four aims — maintaining peace, developing friendly relations, achieving international cooperation, and harmonising actions — and Article 2 states the principles, chief among them the sovereign equality of all members, meaning every nation regardless of size has equal legal standing. On its face, sovereign equality means India, with over a billion people, and a small island nation have the same one vote in the General Assembly. This principle was a direct response to the League of Nations' failure, where the absence of major powers — the United States never joined, and Japan and Germany withdrew — meant the League could not enforce its decisions, as shown by its inability to stop Japan's invasion of Manchuria in 1931 or Italy's invasion of Abyssinia in 1935. The founders learned that an organisation without the backing of the most powerful states is powerless, because enforcement requires military and economic capacity that only major powers possess. The veto power given to the five permanent members — China, France, the USSR, the UK, and the USA — was the price extracted for their continued participation. Without the veto, the major powers would likely have refused to join, repeating the League's fatal weakness; with the veto, the UN secured their membership but created a structural imbalance where a single permanent member can block any substantive Security Council resolution, even when the other 14 members and the vast majority of the General Assembly support it. In practice, sovereign equality holds in the General Assembly but not in the Security Council, where five nations have a legal power the other 188 do not. The veto has been used to shield allies of permanent members from sanctions or intervention, which critics argue contradicts the Charter's own principle that all members shall settle disputes peacefully. However, the counter-argument is that the veto prevents the UN from being used against any major power, which would cause them to withdraw and collapse the system as happened with the League; the veto keeps the powerful inside the tent, where they can be persuaded, rather than outside, where they cannot be constrained. India, as a founding member and one of the largest troop contributors to UN peacekeeping (over 200,000 troops to more than 40 missions since 1948), has consistently called for Security Council reform, arguing that the veto of five nations chosen in 1945 no longer reflects the global distribution of power. India's Article 51 of the Constitution, which promotes international peace and security, reflects its commitment to the UN's aims even as it advocates for reform. In conclusion, the veto was a necessary compromise essential to the UN's founding in 1945 — without it the organisation would likely not exist — but it remains a fundamental contradiction of sovereign equality in practice, and the ongoing reform debate, led by nations like India, reflects the unresolved tension between great-power cooperation and the legal ideal of equal standing for all.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Imagine you are an Indian delegate at the San Francisco Conference in June 1945, representing a country that has just emerged from colonial rule negotiations and is about to sign the UN Charter. Using the facts you have learned, write a short speech (120-150 words) to the conference that includes the date of the conference, the number of nations present, at least two aims and two principles of the Charter you are signing, and a reference to India's constitutional commitment to international peace.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Distinguished delegates, we gather here at San Francisco in June 1945, representatives of 50 nations, to sign a Charter that must succeed where the League of Nations failed. Two world wars in thirty years have killed tens of millions; we cannot permit a third. India signs this Charter because its aims — maintaining international peace and security, and achieving international cooperation in solving humanitarian problems — are aims we already hold. Its principles — the sovereign equality of all members, and the peaceful settlement of disputes — are rules we intend to uphold. Our own Constitution, now being drafted, will include Article 51, directing our State to promote international peace and security and to foster respect for international law. We pledge our troops, our cooperation, and our voice to this United Nations. Let the failures of Manchuria and Abyssinia never be repeated.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a one-page revision chart for the Aims and Principles of the United Nations that includes: (a) the founding details — conference name, dates, founding date, number of members, five permanent members; (b) the four aims of Article 1 in a table with a one-line explanation of each; (c) the four principles of Article 2 in a table with a one-line explanation of each; (d) a 100-word closing paragraph explaining why the UN replaced the League of Nations and how India's Article 51 connects to the UN's aims.
diagnosticQuestions.answer:
Revision chart for the Aims and Principles of the United Nations:

(a) Founding details:
- Conference: San Francisco Conference, April-June 1945
- Original signatories: 50 nations (Poland signed later, total 51 founding members)
- Founding date: 24 October 1945 (UN Day)
- Five permanent members: China, France, USSR (now Russia), United Kingdom, United States
- India: founding member, represented by Sir Arcot Ramaswamy Mudaliar

(b) Four Aims (Article 1 of the UN Charter):
| Aim | Explanation |
| 1. Maintain international peace and security | The UN uses collective action to prevent and remove threats to peace and suppress acts of aggression. |
| 2. Develop friendly relations among nations | Based on respect for equal rights and the self-determination of peoples. |
| 3. Achieve international cooperation | In solving economic, social, cultural, and humanitarian problems worldwide. |
| 4. Harmonise the actions of nations | The UN serves as a centre where member states coordinate their efforts to achieve these common ends. |

(c) Four Principles (Article 2 of the UN Charter):
| Principle | Explanation |
| 1. Sovereign equality of all members | Every member state, large or small, has equal legal standing in the organisation. |
| 2. Peaceful settlement of disputes | All members shall settle their international disputes by peaceful means, not force. |
| 3. Non-use of force | Members shall refrain from the threat or use of force against any state's territorial integrity or political independence. |
| 4. Assistance to the UN | All members shall give the United Nations every assistance in any action it takes. |

(d) Closing paragraph: The United Nations replaced the League of Nations because the League, founded in 1919, failed to stop Japan's invasion of Manchuria in 1931 and Italy's invasion of Abyssinia in 1935, and could not prevent World War II (1939-1945), which killed an estimated 70 to 85 million people. The UN, founded on 24 October 1945 with stronger collective security mechanisms, was designed to correct the League's weaknesses. India's Article 51 of the Constitution, a Directive Principle, directly mirrors the UN's aims by directing the State to promote international peace and security and foster respect for international law — showing that India's domestic constitutional commitment and its UN Charter obligations are one and the same.

masteryCriteria: Can state the full name of the United Nations and the year and date it was founded (24 October 1945), the San Francisco Conference (April-June 1945) where 50 nations signed the Charter (51 with Poland), and the five permanent members of the Security Council (China, France, USSR, UK, USA). Can list at least four aims of the UN as given in Article 1 of the Charter (maintaining international peace and security, developing friendly relations among nations, achieving international cooperation, harmonising the actions of nations) and distinguish them from at least four principles given in Article 2 (sovereign equality of all members, peaceful settlement of disputes, non-use of force, assistance to the UN). Can explain why the UN replaced the League of Nations after its failure to prevent World War II, citing specific failures such as Japan's invasion of Manchuria (1931) and Italy's invasion of Abyssinia (1935). Can connect India's founding membership and Article 51 of the Indian Constitution to the UN's aims, noting India's contribution of over 200,000 troops to UN peacekeeping missions.

title: Organs of the UN — General Assembly and Security Council (Composition and Functions)
subject: histciv
definition: The United Nations Charter, signed on 26 June 1945 at the San Francisco Conference and entering into force on 24 October 1945, established six principal organs through which the world body functions: the General Assembly, the Security Council, the Economic and Social Council, the Trusteeship Council, the International Court of Justice, and the Secretariat. This node focuses on the first two — the General Assembly and the Security Council — which together embody the tension between democratic representation and executive enforcement at the heart of the UN's design. The General Assembly, defined in Chapter IV of the Charter (Articles 9 to 22), is the deliberative and representative organ in which all 193 member states (as of 2024) sit with equal status. Each member state has one vote, regardless of size, wealth, or military power — a principle of sovereign equality that means India's vote carries the same formal weight as the vote of the United States, China, or Tuvalu. The Assembly meets in regular session each year from September to December at UN Headquarters in New York, and its President is elected for a one-year term on a rotational basis among the five regional groups. Its functions are broad: it discusses any question within the scope of the Charter and makes recommendations to member states or to the Security Council; it considers and approves the UN budget and apportions expenses among members; it elects the non-permanent members of the Security Council, members of the Economic and Social Council, and judges of the International Court of Justice; and it admits new member states on the recommendation of the Security Council. Crucially, General Assembly resolutions on international peace and security are recommendatory, not legally binding — they carry moral and political weight but cannot compel a state to act, except on internal matters such as the budget and admissions. The Security Council, defined in Chapter V (Articles 23 to 32), is the executive organ with primary responsibility for maintaining international peace and security. It has 15 members: 5 permanent — China, France, the Russian Federation, the United Kingdom, and the United States (the P5, reflecting the victorious powers of the Second World War) — and 10 non-permanent members elected by the General Assembly for two-year terms, allocated geographically to ensure regional representation. The P5 each hold veto power under Article 27: on substantive matters, a single "no" vote from any permanent member blocks action, regardless of how many other members vote in favour. Abstention, however, is not a veto — a P5 member that abstains does not block a resolution, a distinction frequently misunderstood. The Security Council's functions include investigating disputes and making recommendations for peaceful settlement, imposing economic sanctions and arms embargoes, and authorising collective military action — powers that make its resolutions binding on all member states under Article 25. India has been elected as a non-permanent member eight times, most recently for the 2021-2022 term, reflecting its active engagement with the Council despite its long-standing aspiration for permanent membership through the G4 initiative alongside Brazil, Germany, and Japan. The contrast between the two organs is stark: the General Assembly is universal, democratic, and recommendatory; the Security Council is selective, executive, and binding — a design that reflects the post-1945 conviction that peace enforcement must not be paralysed by endless debate, but which also concentrates extraordinary power in five states.
eli5: Imagine your school has two committees. The first is a General Meeting (the General Assembly) where every single student from every class sits and votes — one vote each, whether you are in Class 1 or Class 12 (all 193 member states have one vote each, regardless of size). They can discuss anything and pass opinions (resolutions), but the principal is not forced to obey them (General Assembly resolutions are recommendations, not binding). The second is a small Security Committee (the Security Council) of fifteen students — five senior prefects (the permanent members: USA, UK, France, Russia, and China) who can never be removed and can block any decision single-handedly by saying "no" (the veto power), plus ten others (non-permanent members) chosen for two years. Whatever this committee decides (under Chapter VII of the UN Charter), everyone must follow — its decisions are legally binding on all member states. That is the General Assembly and the Security Council of the UN, the two most important organs.

diagnosticQuestions.question: List the six principal organs of the United Nations. State the composition of the General Assembly and the Security Council, including the number of members, the voting rule for each, and the names of the five permanent members of the Security Council.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The six principal organs of the United Nations are the General Assembly, the Security Council, the Economic and Social Council, the Trusteeship Council, the International Court of Justice, and the Secretariat. The General Assembly comprises all 193 member states of the UN (as of 2024), each with one vote regardless of size or power — the principle of sovereign equality. It meets in regular session annually from September to December at UN Headquarters in New York. The Security Council has 15 members: 5 permanent and 10 non-permanent. The five permanent members are China, France, the Russian Federation, the United Kingdom, and the United States — collectively known as the P5. Each permanent member holds veto power under Article 27 of the Charter, meaning a single "no" vote from any one of them blocks a substantive resolution. The 10 non-permanent members are elected by the General Assembly for two-year terms. A substantive resolution in the Security Council requires nine affirmative votes out of fifteen, including no veto from any permanent member. The General Assembly votes by simple majority on most matters and a two-thirds majority on important questions such as the admission of new members, budgetary decisions, and recommendations on peace and security.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Why does the General Assembly have 193 members with one vote each while the Security Council has only 15 members, five of whom hold a veto? Explain how this design reflects the UN Charter's twin aims of sovereign equality and effective peace enforcement, and why the General Assembly's resolutions are recommendatory while the Security Council's are binding.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The different compositions and powers of the two organs reflect a deliberate compromise in the UN Charter between two values that are in tension: democratic equality and executive effectiveness. The General Assembly embodies sovereign equality — the principle, stated in Article 2(1) of the Charter, that all member states are equal. Giving all 193 members one vote each, regardless of size, wealth, or military power, ensures that every nation has a voice and that the UN is not a club of the powerful. India's vote carries the same formal weight as that of the United States. However, if the General Assembly's resolutions on peace and security were binding, a simple majority of small states could compel large powers to act against their will, which would drive the powerful states out of the organisation — precisely what happened to the League of Nations, which lacked enforcement power and failed. The Security Council therefore takes the opposite design: a small body of 15 members that can act quickly and decisively, with resolutions binding on all member states under Article 25. The five permanent members — China, France, Russia, the UK, and the USA — were the principal victorious powers of the Second World War and, at the time, the world's strongest military powers. Granting them the veto ensured that they would remain in the UN rather than walk out, because no enforcement action could be taken against their wishes. This was a pragmatic recognition of power realities: an enforcement body that could order the strongest states around would simply be ignored or destroyed. The trade-off is that the veto can paralyse the Council — as in February 2022, when Russia vetoed a resolution condemning its own invasion of Ukraine. The General Assembly then passed a non-binding resolution with 141 votes in favour, showing that the Assembly provides a moral voice that cannot be silenced by a single veto, even though it cannot compel action. The two organs thus complement each other: the Assembly provides democratic legitimacy and universal representation; the Council provides the capacity for binding enforcement, accepting the risk of paralysis in exchange for keeping the great powers at the table.

diagnosticQuestions.question: "The veto power of the five permanent members of the Security Council is both the greatest strength and the greatest weakness of the United Nations." Evaluate this statement with reference to the composition of the Security Council (5 permanent and 10 non-permanent members), the binding authority of Council resolutions under Article 25, the February 2022 Ukraine veto, the General Assembly's recommendatory resolution with 141 votes, and India's eight terms as a non-permanent member and its campaign for permanent membership through the G4. Argue whether the veto should be retained, reformed, or abolished.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The statement captures the central paradox of the UN's design. The veto is the Security Council's greatest strength because it keeps the five most powerful states — China, France, Russia, the UK, and the USA — inside the organisation. The Charter was drafted in 1945 in the shadow of the League of Nations' failure, which was caused in part by the absence of major powers: the United States never joined, Germany and Japan withdrew, and the Soviet Union was expelled. The veto guarantees that no enforcement action can be taken against a P5 member's will, so the strongest states have no incentive to leave. Without the veto, a binding resolution could be passed against a great power, which would either ignore it — destroying the Council's credibility — or withdraw, destroying the UN itself. The veto also ensures that the Council's binding authority under Article 25 is exercised with the consent of the powers capable of enforcing it, making its resolutions credible rather than paper commands. In this sense, the veto is the price of great-power participation, and that participation is the foundation of the UN's survival for nearly eight decades. However, the veto is also the Council's greatest weakness because it allows any single permanent member to block action on the most serious threats to international peace, including acts of aggression by a P5 member itself. The clearest recent illustration is February 2022: Russia invaded Ukraine, the Security Council attempted to pass a resolution condemning the invasion, and Russia vetoed it. The Council was paralysed by the very mechanism designed to keep it functional. The General Assembly then passed a non-binding resolution with 141 votes in favour, condemning the invasion — but this resolution could not authorise sanctions, military action, or any binding measure, because only the Security Council has that power. The result was that the UN's executive organ was unable to act on a clear breach of the Charter while its deliberative organ could only express opinion. India's experience illustrates the frustration of the broader membership. India has served as a non-permanent member eight times, most recently in 2021-2022, contributing troops to peacekeeping and participating actively in Council debates, yet it remains excluded from permanent membership and the veto. Along with Brazil, Germany, and Japan — the G4 — India has campaigned for expansion of the permanent membership, but any Charter amendment requires the consent of all five current P5 members, each of whom can veto its own enlargement, creating a Catch-22. The "United for Consensus" group, led by Italy, Pakistan, and others, opposes expansion, further stalling reform. On balance, the veto should not be abolished outright, because doing so risks great-power withdrawal and a return to pre-1945 anarchy. But it should be reformed: the most widely supported proposal is that the veto should not apply in cases of genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity — the "Responsibility to Protect" principle — and that the permanent membership should be expanded to include India, Brazil, Germany, Japan, and African representation, so that the Council reflects the geopolitical realities of the 21st century rather than the aftermath of a war fought eighty years ago. The veto's retention is defensible only if it is constrained and if the Council's composition is modernised; without reform, the gap between the Council's binding authority and its democratic legitimacy will continue to widen.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Imagine you are India's Permanent Representative to the United Nations in February 2022. The Security Council has just failed to pass a resolution condemning Russia's invasion of Ukraine because Russia vetoed it. Using the facts you have learned, write a short briefing note (120-150 words) for the Ministry of External Affairs in New Delhi explaining what happened in the Security Council, what the General Assembly did next, how India voted, and what this episode reveals about the difference between the two organs' powers.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Briefing Note, New York, February 2022 — The Security Council today voted on a resolution condemning the Russian Federation's invasion of Ukraine. The resolution received the required nine affirmative votes but was blocked by a veto from Russia, a permanent member exercising its Article 27 power. As is well known, a single "no" from any P5 member defeats a substantive resolution regardless of the majority. The matter will now move to the General Assembly under the "Uniting for Peace" procedure, where a resolution condemning the invasion is expected to pass with a large majority — 141 votes in favour — but will be recommendatory, not binding, since only the Security Council can impose sanctions or authorise military action under Article 25. This episode starkly illustrates the difference between the two organs: the Council has binding authority but can be paralysed by one veto; the Assembly has universal membership and moral weight but cannot compel action. India should consider its vote carefully.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a one-page comparison table of the General Assembly and the Security Council with at least eight rows covering membership, voting rules, session frequency, binding authority, key functions, election of members, the role of the veto, and one real-world example for each organ. Then write a 100-word closing paragraph explaining why the two organs' different designs are both necessary for the UN to function.
diagnosticQuestions.answer:
Comparison table: General Assembly vs Security Council

1. Membership: General Assembly — all 193 member states, one vote each. Security Council — 15 members (5 permanent, 10 non-permanent).
2. Permanent members: General Assembly — none; all members are equal. Security Council — 5 permanent (China, France, Russia, UK, USA) with veto under Article 27.
3. Non-permanent members: General Assembly — not applicable. Security Council — 10 elected by the General Assembly for two-year terms on a regional basis.
4. Voting rule: General Assembly — simple majority on most matters, two-thirds majority on important questions. Security Council — nine out of fifteen affirmative votes on substantive matters, with no veto from any P5 member; procedural matters require nine votes with no veto.
5. Session frequency: General Assembly — regular annual session from September to December, plus special and emergency special sessions. Security Council — functions continuously; meets whenever called by the Secretary-General or any member.
6. Binding authority: General Assembly — resolutions are recommendatory except on internal matters (budget, admissions). Security Council — resolutions are binding on all member states under Article 25.
7. Key functions: General Assembly — discusses any Charter matter and makes recommendations, approves the budget, elects non-permanent Security Council members, admits new members. Security Council — investigates disputes, recommends peaceful settlement, imposes sanctions, authorises collective military action.
8. Real-world example: General Assembly — February 2022 non-binding resolution condemning Russia's invasion of Ukraine with 141 votes in favour. Security Council — Resolution 84 (1950) authorising military action under UN command during the Korean War; February 2022 veto by Russia blocking the Ukraine condemnation resolution.

Closing paragraph: The two organs' different designs are both necessary because the UN must balance democratic representation with effective enforcement. The General Assembly, with all 193 members and one vote each, gives every nation a voice and ensures the organisation's legitimacy — but its recommendatory resolutions cannot compel action, because a majority of small states cannot order great powers around. The Security Council, with only 15 members and binding authority, can act decisively to maintain peace — but the P5 veto ensures the strongest states remain at the table rather than withdrawing, as they did from the League of Nations. Without the Assembly, the UN would lack legitimacy; without the Council, it would lack enforcement power. Both designs are imperfect, but together they make the UN functional.

Can describe the composition of the General Assembly — all 193 member states with one vote each, meeting in regular annual session from September to December at UN Headquarters in New York — and list at least three of its functions including discussing and recommending on international issues, approving the UN budget, and electing non-permanent Security Council members.
